$$
f(x; \theta) = (\theta+1) x^{-\theta-2}, \qquad x \geq 1,
$$

where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter. Find the likelihood function of the sample $2.0, \, 4.5, \,5.1 .$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x; \theta),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is

$$
L(\theta) = P(X_1=x_1, X_2=x_2, \ldots , X_n = x_n) = \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta).
$$

$$
f(x; \theta) = (\theta+1) x^{-\theta-2}, \qquad x \geq 1.
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}((\theta +1){x}_{i}^{-\theta -2}) \\  & =(\theta +1)^{n}\cdot {\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{-\theta -2} \\  & =(\theta +1)^{n}({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i})^{-\theta -2}\end{aligned}
$$

For our sample, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =2.0\cdot 4.5\cdot 5.1=45.9\end{aligned}
$$

and $n=3.$ Therefore, 

$$
L(\theta) = (\theta+1)^{3} ( 45.9 )^{-\theta-2}.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192797 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-1983f891-c0ec-5f2f-97f4-aee1cde66c6b" "question-722785f1-98e4-52e2-9870-cc5147d770a3" "question-d0ac51fa-7d6b-5afa-a10b-159234b28e9a" "question-7d257a6c-5e5c-58a0-af13-fdf60799b0d8" "question-bc819016-9ccb-568a-b71d-77c2cc9598ca"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192521 :question/problem "Suppose $X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_6$ is an I.I.D random sample with $X_i \sim \text{Exp}(\theta)$ and unknown rate parameter $\theta.$ Find the likelihood function of the sample $1.5, \, 2.0, \, 1.1, \, 0.4, \, 3.3, \, 2.7.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x; \theta),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is

$$
L(\theta) = P(X_1=x_1, X_2=x_2, \ldots , X_n = x_n) = \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta).
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=6$ independent exponential random variables with unknown parameter $\theta,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x; \,\theta) = \theta e^{-\theta x}, \qquad x\geq 0.
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}\theta {e}^{-\theta {x}_{i}} \\  & =(\theta {e}^{-\theta {x}_{1}})\cdot (\theta {e}^{-\theta {x}_{2}})⋯(\theta {e}^{-\theta {x}_{n}}) \\  & ={\theta }^{n}\,{e}^{-\theta ({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+⋯+{x}_{n})} \\  & ={\theta }^{n}\,{e}^{-\theta \sum {x}_{i}} \\  & ={\theta }^{n}\,{e}^{-S\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

where $\displaystyle S = \sum\limits_ {i=1}^n x_i.$ 

For our sample, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =1.5+2.0+1.1+0.4+3.3+2.7 \\  & =11\end{aligned}
$$

and $n=6.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\theta }^{6}\,{e}^{-11\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192684 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-5ede7a13-53b1-5dcd-b174-1b2115493b08" "question-0b9cdfe0-b9cf-519c-9814-c1b778856085" "question-2015b9da-5691-5067-96fe-7987a1cb7888" "question-48c555e3-358d-5d44-81b1-fa7fdd197fa6" "question-2f4678d5-a087-5e11-90cc-f482d76b03ff"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192389 :question/problem "Suppose $X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4$ is an I.I.D random sample with $X_i \sim N(\theta, 1),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown mean. Find the likelihood function of the sample $0.4,\, -0.3,\, -2.2,\, -0.4.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x; \theta),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is

$$
L(\theta) = P(X_1=x_1, X_2=x_2, \ldots , X_n = x_n) = \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta).
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta$ and variance $\sigma^2 = 1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x; \theta) = \dfrac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{x-\theta}{\sigma} \right)^2} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(x-\theta)^2/2}, \qquad x \in (-\infty,\infty).
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-\sum ({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(\sum {x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta \sum {x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(C-2S\theta +n{\theta }^{2})/2}\end{aligned}
$$

where $\displaystyle S = \sum\limits_ {i=1}^n x_i$ and $\displaystyle C = \sum\limits_ {i=1}^n x_i^2.$

For our sample, we have that $n=4,$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =0.4+(-0.3)+(-2.2)+(-0.4) \\  & =-2.5 \\ C & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2} \\  & =(0.4)^{2}+(-0.3)^{2}+(-2.2)^{2}+(-0.4)^{2} \\  & =5.25\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & =(2\pi )^{-4/2}\,{e}^{-(5.25-2(-2.5)\theta +4{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4{\pi }^{2}}\,{e}^{-2.625\,-\,2.5\theta \,-\,2{\theta }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-0a61b26d-5077-52d9-9883-5f2b02dfb768" :question/id #uuid "0a61b26d-5077-52d9-9883-5f2b02dfb768" :question/math-academy-id "q-159900" :question/problem "Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{18}$ be I.I.D. random variables with probability density function

$$
f(x;\theta )=\theta {x}^{-\theta -1},\,x\ge 1,
$$

where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter. For a particular sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{18},$ you're given that 

$$
{\prod }_{i=1}^{18}{x}_{i}=34.2.
$$

Find the likelihood function of the sample." :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
L(\theta )=P({X}_{1}={x}_{1},{X}_{2}={x}_{2},…,{X}_{n}={x}_{n})={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\,\theta ).
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=18$ independent random variables with unknown parameter $\theta ,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x;\theta )=\theta {x}^{-\theta -1},\,x\ge 1.
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\theta {x}_{i}^{-\theta -1}) \\  & ={\theta }^{n}\cdot {\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{-\theta -1} \\  & ={\theta }^{n}({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i})^{-\theta -1}\end{aligned}
$$

We are told that ${\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}=34.2$ and $n=18.$ Therefore, 

$$
L(\theta )={\theta }^{18}(34.2)^{-\theta -1}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b7072343-82c3-507f-9cad-e945e7d13486"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

$$
f(x;\theta )=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-\sum ({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(\sum {x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta \sum {x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(C-2S\theta +n{\theta }^{2})/2}\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}$ and $C={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}.$

We are told that $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}=-2.8,$ $C={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}=14.24,$ and $n=10.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & =(2\pi )^{-10/2}\,{e}^{-(14.24-2(-2.8)\theta +10{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{32{\pi }^{5}}\,{e}^{\,-7.12\,-\,2.8\theta \,-\,5{\theta }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

"question-2f4678d5-a087-5e11-90cc-f482d76b03ff" :question/id #uuid "2f4678d5-a087-5e11-90cc-f482d76b03ff" :question/math-academy-id "q-159955" :question/problem "Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},{X}_{3},{X}_{4},{X}_{5}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼N(\theta ,1),$  where $\theta $ is an unknown mean.  Given that the likelihood function of the sample $1.3,\,0.2,\,2.3,\,-0.7,\,0.9$ is

$$
L(\theta )=\frac{1}{(2\pi )^{5/2}}\,{e}^{\,g(\theta )},
$$

what is the expression for $g(\theta )?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
L(\theta )=P({X}_{1}={x}_{1},{X}_{2}={x}_{2},…,{X}_{n}={x}_{n})={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\,\theta ).
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=5$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta $ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x;\theta )=\frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{x-\theta }{\sigma })}^{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-\sum ({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(\sum {x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta \sum {x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(C-2S\theta +n{\theta }^{2})/2}\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}$ and $C={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}.$

For our sample, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =1.3+0.2+2.7+(-0.7)+0.9 \\  & =4 \\ C & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2} \\  & =(1.3)^{2}+(0.2)^{2}+(2.3)^{2}+(-0.7)^{2}+(0.9)^{2} \\  & =8.32\end{aligned}
$$

and $n=5.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & =(2\pi )^{-5/2}\,{e}^{-(8.32-2(4)\theta +5{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{(2\pi )^{5/2}}\,{e}^{\,-4.16\,+\,4\theta \,-\,2.5{\theta }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
g(\theta )=-4.16+4\theta -2.5{\theta }^{2}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f3360e07-7504-5830-8a53-b33be132c97b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f3360e07-7504-5830-8a53-b33be132c97b" :answer-field/id #uuid "f3360e07-7504-5830-8a53-b33be132c97b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-946fb421-d9f8-515c-ac0d-2febe8130990" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d02565f7-fd05-587b-984b-2ec02701ae9c" "answer-ac7b1eee-2e2d-566b-b6cb-2cd855b3f405" "answer-c57acc65-7f21-5f64-86dc-1d888225d7cf" "answer-946fb421-d9f8-515c-ac0d-2febe8130990" "answer-ee68ad46-6e17-52dc-b4f9-939c7a0635ea"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d02565f7-fd05-587b-984b-2ec02701ae9c" :answer/id #uuid "d02565f7-fd05-587b-984b-2ec02701ae9c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1+4\theta -2.5{\theta }^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ac7b1eee-2e2d-566b-b6cb-2cd855b3f405" :answer/id #uuid "ac7b1eee-2e2d-566b-b6cb-2cd855b3f405" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1+4\theta -5{\theta }^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c57acc65-7f21-5f64-86dc-1d888225d7cf" :answer/id #uuid "c57acc65-7f21-5f64-86dc-1d888225d7cf" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-4+5\theta -{\theta }^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-946fb421-d9f8-515c-ac0d-2febe8130990" :answer/id #uuid "946fb421-d9f8-515c-ac0d-2febe8130990" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-4.16+4\theta -2.5{\theta }^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ee68ad46-6e17-52dc-b4f9-939c7a0635ea" :answer/id #uuid "ee68ad46-6e17-52dc-b4f9-939c7a0635ea" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-8.32+5\theta -{\theta }^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193897 :tutorial/content "Likelihood functions of samples drawn from populations modeled using continuous random variables are defined similarly to discrete variables. The only difference is that we use probability density functions instead of probability mass functions.

If $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed *continuous* random variables with probability density function $f(x; \theta),$ then the likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is given by

$$
L(\theta) = P(X_1=x_1, X_2=x_2, \ldots , X_n = x_n) = \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta).
$$

For example, let $X_1, X_2, X_3$ be continuous, I.I.D. random variables with the following probability density function:

$$
f(x; \theta) = \theta x^{-\theta-1}, \qquad x \geq 1
$$

Here, $\theta$ is an unknown parameter. Suppose we conduct our random sample and get the following results:

$$
x_1 = 2.5, \qquad x_2 = 3.2, \qquad x_3 = 1.2.
$$

 

In this case, we compute the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\theta {x}_{i}^{-\theta -1}) \\  & =(\theta {x}_{1}^{-\theta -1})\cdot (\theta {x}_{2}^{-\theta -1})⋯(\theta {x}_{n}^{-\theta -1}) \\  & ={\theta }^{n}({x}_{1}^{-\theta -1})\cdot ({x}_{2}^{-\theta -1})⋯({x}_{n}^{-\theta -1}) \\  & ={\theta }^{n}{({x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}⋯{x}_{n})}^{-\theta -1} \\  & ={\theta }^{n}({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i})^{-\theta -1}\end{aligned}
$$

For our sample, we have $n=3$, and

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =2.5\cdot 3.2\cdot 1.2=9.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
L(\theta) = \theta^{3} ( 9.6 )^{-\theta-1}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193902 :tutorial/content "The probability density function of a normally distributed random variable $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ is given by

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac12\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2}.
$$

Some example normal distribution curves are shown below. 

![](images/c9/c9359fc84401aabb19e526755b70647cb0496fa8ddba65974466e0ffc3dbbbdc.png)

If we set $\sigma=1,$ then $f(x)$ simplifies as follows:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2}.
$$

This is a standard normal random variable whose mean is shifted right by $\mu$ units.

Finally, setting the unknown parameter as $\theta$ when discussing likelihood functions is common. Following this convention, we set $\mu=\theta,$ and we get

$$
f(x;\theta) =  \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-\theta)^2/2}.
$$

Let's use this to compute some likelihood functions of some normally distributed sample data." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192932 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

Find the likelihood function of the sample $0.4,\, -0.3,\, -2.2,\, -0.4.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x; \theta),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is

"question-5ede7a13-53b1-5dcd-b174-1b2115493b08" :question/id #uuid "5ede7a13-53b1-5dcd-b174-1b2115493b08" :question/math-academy-id "q-159953" :question/problem "Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{10}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼N(\theta ,1),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown mean. For a particular sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{10},$ you're given that 

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{10}{x}_{i}=-2.8,\,{\sum }_{i=1}^{10}{x}_{i}^{2}=14.24.
$$

Given that the likelihood function of the sample is

$$
L(\theta )=\frac{1}{32{\pi }^{5}}\,{e}^{\,g(\theta )},
$$

what is the expression for $g(\theta )?$

*Hint: The probability density function for a normal random variable with mean $\theta $ and variance $1$ is given by* 

$$
f(x;\theta )=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
L(\theta )=P({X}_{1}={x}_{1},{X}_{2}={x}_{2},…,{X}_{n}={x}_{n})={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\,\theta ).
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=10$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta $ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x;\theta )=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-\sum ({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(\sum {x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta \sum {x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(C-2S\theta +n{\theta }^{2})/2}\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}$ and $C={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}.$

We are told that $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}=-2.8,$ $C={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}=14.24,$ and $n=10.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & =(2\pi )^{-10/2}\,{e}^{-(14.24-2(-2.8)\theta +10{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{32{\pi }^{5}}\,{e}^{\,-7.12\,-\,2.8\theta \,-\,5{\theta }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
g(\theta )=-7.12-2.8\theta -5{\theta }^{2}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b6084e73-2e8b-5dd9-9cce-558327c71c52"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Given that the likelihood function of the sample $4.8,\,0.7,\,5.0,\,2.7,\,1.9,\,2.7$ is

$$
L(\theta )=\frac{1}{8{\pi }^{3}}\,{e}^{\,g(\theta )},
$$

what is the expression for $g(\theta )?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
L(\theta )=P({X}_{1}={x}_{1},{X}_{2}={x}_{2},…,{X}_{n}={x}_{n})={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\,\theta ).
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=6$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta $ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x;\theta )=\frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{x-\theta }{\sigma })}^{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-\sum ({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(\sum {x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta \sum {x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(C-2S\theta +n{\theta }^{2})/2}\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}$ and $C={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}.$

For our sample, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =4.8+0.7+5+2.7+1.9+2.7 \\  & =17.8 \\ C & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2} \\  & =(4.8)^{2}+(0.7)^{2}+(5)^{2}+(2.7)^{2}+(1.9)^{2}+(2.7)^{2} \\  & =66.72\end{aligned}
$$

and $n=6.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & =(2\pi )^{-6/2}\,{e}^{-(66.72-2(17.8)\theta +6{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{8{\pi }^{3}}\,{e}^{\,-33.36\,+\,17.8\theta \,-\,3{\theta }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
g(\theta )=-33.36+17.8\theta -3{\theta }^{2}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-273285e8-0feb-51b2-b1b4-ca3ec40e4303"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id The only difference is that we use probability density functions instead of probability mass functions.

If $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed *continuous* random variables with probability density function $f(x; \theta),$ then the likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is given by

$$
L(\theta) = P(X_1=x_1, X_2=x_2, \ldots , X_n = x_n) = \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta).
$$

For example, let $X_1, X_2, X_3$ be continuous, I.I.D. random variables with the following probability density function:

$$
f(x; \theta) = \theta x^{-\theta-1}, \qquad x \geq 1
$$

Here, $\theta$ is an unknown parameter. Suppose we conduct our random sample and get the following results:

$$
x_1 = 2.5, \qquad x_2 = 3.2, \qquad x_3 = 1.2.
$$

 

In this case, we compute the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\theta {x}_{i}^{-\theta -1}) \\  & =(\theta {x}_{1}^{-\theta -1})\cdot (\theta {x}_{2}^{-\theta -1})⋯(\theta {x}_{n}^{-\theta -1}) \\  & ={\theta }^{n}({x}_{1}^{-\theta -1})\cdot ({x}_{2}^{-\theta -1})⋯({x}_{n}^{-\theta -1}) \\  & ={\theta }^{n}{({x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}⋯{x}_{n})}^{-\theta -1} \\  & ={\theta }^{n}({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i})^{-\theta -1}\end{aligned}
$$

For our sample, we have $n=3$, and

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =2.5\cdot 3.2\cdot 1.2=9.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
L(\theta) = \theta^{3} ( 9.6 )^{-\theta-1}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193902 :tutorial/content "The probability density function of a normally distributed random variable $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ is given by

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac12\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2}.
$$

Some example normal distribution curves are shown below. 

![](images/c9/c9359fc84401aabb19e526755b70647cb0496fa8ddba65974466e0ffc3dbbbdc.png)

If we set $\sigma=1,$ then $f(x)$ simplifies as follows:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2}.
$$

This is a standard normal random variable whose mean is shifted right by $\mu$ units.

Finally, setting the unknown parameter as $\theta$ when discussing likelihood functions is common. Following this convention, we set $\mu=\theta,$ and we get

$$
f(x;\theta) =  \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-\theta)^2/2}.
$$

:question/problem "Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{10}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼N(\theta ,1),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown mean. For a particular sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{10},$ you're given that 

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{10}{x}_{i}=-2.8,\,{\sum }_{i=1}^{10}{x}_{i}^{2}=14.24.
$$

Given that the likelihood function of the sample is

$$
L(\theta )=\frac{1}{32{\pi }^{5}}\,{e}^{\,g(\theta )},
$$

what is the expression for $g(\theta )?$

*Hint: The probability density function for a normal random variable with mean $\theta $ and variance $1$ is given by* 

$$
f(x;\theta )=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$"] ["question-5ede7a13-53b1-5dcd-b174-1b2115493b08" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
L(\theta )=P({X}_{1}={x}_{1},{X}_{2}={x}_{2},…,{X}_{n}={x}_{n})={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\,\theta ).
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=10$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta $ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x;\theta )=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-\sum ({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(\sum {x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta \sum {x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(C-2S\theta +n{\theta }^{2})/2}\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}$ and $C={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}.$

We are told that $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}=-2.8,$ $C={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}=14.24,$ and $n=10.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & =(2\pi )^{-10/2}\,{e}^{-(14.24-2(-2.8)\theta +10{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{32{\pi }^{5}}\,{e}^{\,-7.12\,-\,2.8\theta \,-\,5{\theta }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
g(\theta )=-7.12-2.8\theta -5{\theta }^{2}.
$$"] ["question-5ede7a13-53b1-5dcd-b174-1b2115493b08" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-b6084e73-2e8b-5dd9-9cce-558327c71c52" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{8}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼N(\theta ,1),$  where $\theta $ is an unknown mean. For a particular sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{8},$ you're given that 

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{8}{x}_{i}=5.6,\,{\sum }_{i=1}^{8}{x}_{i}^{2}=7.8.
$$

Given that the likelihood function of the sample is

$$
L(\theta )=\frac{1}{16{\pi }^{4}}\,{e}^{\,g(\theta )},
$$

what is the expression for $g(\theta )?$

*Hint: The probability density function for a normal random variable with mean $\theta $ and variance $1$ is given by* 

$$
f(x;\theta )=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$"] ["question-0b9cdfe0-b9cf-519c-9814-c1b778856085" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
L(\theta )=P({X}_{1}={x}_{1},{X}_{2}={x}_{2},…,{X}_{n}={x}_{n})={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\,\theta ).
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=8$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta $ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x;\theta )=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-\sum ({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(\sum {x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta \sum {x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(C-2S\theta +n{\theta }^{2})/2}\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}$ and $C={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}.$

We are told that $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}=5.6,$ $C={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}=7.8,$ and $n=8.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & =(2\pi )^{-8/2}\,{e}^{-(7.8-2(5.6)\theta +8{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{16{\pi }^{4}}\,{e}^{\,-3.9\,+\,5.6\theta \,-\,4{\theta }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
g(\theta )=-3.9+5.6\theta -4{\theta }^{2}.
$$"] ["question-0b9cdfe0-b9cf-519c-9814-c1b778856085" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-9d7c05fc-2a50-5093-8512-b4d447e9981f" :answer-field/id #uuid L(\theta )=P({X}_{1}={x}_{1},{X}_{2}={x}_{2},…,{X}_{n}={x}_{n})={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\,\theta ).

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=6$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta $ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x;\theta )=\frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{x-\theta }{\sigma })}^{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =4.8+0.7+5+2.7+1.9+2.7 \\  & =17.8 \\ C & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2} \\  & =(4.8)^{2}+(0.7)^{2}+(5)^{2}+(2.7)^{2}+(1.9)^{2}+(2.7)^{2} \\  & =66.72\end{aligned}
$$

and $n=6.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & =(2\pi )^{-6/2}\,{e}^{-(66.72-2(17.8)\theta +6{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{8{\pi }^{3}}\,{e}^{\,-33.36\,+\,17.8\theta \,-\,3{\theta }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

:question/problem "Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},{X}_{3},{X}_{4},{X}_{5}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼N(\theta ,1),$  where $\theta $ is an unknown mean.  Given that the likelihood function of the sample $1.3,\,0.2,\,2.3,\,-0.7,\,0.9$ is

$$
L(\theta )=\frac{1}{(2\pi )^{5/2}}\,{e}^{\,g(\theta )},
$$

what is the expression for $g(\theta )?$"] ["question-2f4678d5-a087-5e11-90cc-f482d76b03ff" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
L(\theta )=P({X}_{1}={x}_{1},{X}_{2}={x}_{2},…,{X}_{n}={x}_{n})={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\,\theta ).
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=5$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta $ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x;\theta )=\frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{x-\theta }{\sigma })}^{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-\sum ({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(\sum {x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta \sum {x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(C-2S\theta +n{\theta }^{2})/2}\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}$ and $C={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}.$

For our sample, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =1.3+0.2+2.7+(-0.7)+0.9 \\  & =4 \\ C & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2} \\  & =(1.3)^{2}+(0.2)^{2}+(2.3)^{2}+(-0.7)^{2}+(0.9)^{2} \\  & =8.32\end{aligned}
$$

and $n=5.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & =(2\pi )^{-5/2}\,{e}^{-(8.32-2(4)\theta +5{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{(2\pi )^{5/2}}\,{e}^{\,-4.16\,+\,4\theta \,-\,2.5{\theta }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
g(\theta )=-4.16+4\theta -2.5{\theta }^{2}.
$$"] ["question-2f4678d5-a087-5e11-90cc-f482d76b03ff" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-f3360e07-7504-5830-8a53-b33be132c97b" :answer-field/id #uuid The only difference is that we use probability density functions instead of probability mass functions.

If $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed *continuous* random variables with probability density function $f(x; \theta),$ then the likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is given by

$$
L(\theta) = P(X_1=x_1, X_2=x_2, \ldots , X_n = x_n) = \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta).
$$

For example, let $X_1, X_2, X_3$ be continuous, I.I.D. random variables with the following probability density function:

$$
f(x; \theta) = \theta x^{-\theta-1}, \qquad x \geq 1
$$

Here, $\theta$ is an unknown parameter. Suppose we conduct our random sample and get the following results:

$$
x_1 = 2.5, \qquad x_2 = 3.2, \qquad x_3 = 1.2.
$$

 

In this case, we compute the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\theta {x}_{i}^{-\theta -1}) \\  & =(\theta {x}_{1}^{-\theta -1})\cdot (\theta {x}_{2}^{-\theta -1})⋯(\theta {x}_{n}^{-\theta -1}) \\  & ={\theta }^{n}({x}_{1}^{-\theta -1})\cdot ({x}_{2}^{-\theta -1})⋯({x}_{n}^{-\theta -1}) \\  & ={\theta }^{n}{({x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}⋯{x}_{n})}^{-\theta -1} \\  & ={\theta }^{n}({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i})^{-\theta -1}\end{aligned}
$$

For our sample, we have $n=3$, and

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =2.5\cdot 3.2\cdot 1.2=9.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
L(\theta) = \theta^{3} ( 9.6 )^{-\theta-1}.
$$"] [17592186193902 :tutorial/content "The probability density function of a normally distributed random variable $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ is given by

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac12\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2}.
$$

Some example normal distribution curves are shown below. 

![](images/c9/c9359fc84401aabb19e526755b70647cb0496fa8ddba65974466e0ffc3dbbbdc.png)

If we set $\sigma=1,$ then $f(x)$ simplifies as follows:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2}.
$$

This is a standard normal random variable whose mean is shifted right by $\mu$ units.

Finally, setting the unknown parameter as $\theta$ when discussing likelihood functions is common. Following this convention, we set $\mu=\theta,$ and we get

$$

L(\theta) = P(X_1=x_1, X_2=x_2, \ldots, X_n = x_n) = \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta)
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta$ and variance

$$
\sigma^2 = 1
$$

for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x; \theta) = \dfrac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{x-\theta}{\sigma} \right)^2} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(x-\theta)^2/2}, \qquad x \in (-\infty,\infty)
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
L(θ) &= ∏_(i = 1)^(n)(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2π}}e^{- (x_{i} - θ)^{2}/2}) \\
&= (2π)^{-n/2}e^{- ∑(x_{i} - θ)^{2}/2} \\
&= (2π)^{-n/2}e^{- (∑x_{i}^{2} - 2θ∑x_{i} + nθ^{2})/2} \\
&= (2π)^{-n/2}e^{- (C - 2Sθ + nθ^{2})/2}
\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
\displaystyle S = \sum\limits_ {i=1}^n x_i
$$

and

$$
\displaystyle C = \sum\limits_ {i=1}^n x_i^2
$$

For our sample, we have that $n=4$, and

$$
\begin{aligned}
S &= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} \\
&= 0.4 + (-0.3) + (-2.2) + (-0.4) \\
&=-2.5 \\
C &= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}^{2} \\
&= (0.4)^{2} + (-0.3)^{2} + (-2.2)^{2} + (-0.4)^{2} \\
&= 5.25
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
L(θ) &= (2π)^{-4/2}e^{- (5.25 - 2(-2.5)θ + 4θ^{2})/2} \\
&= \frac{1}{4π^{2}}e^{-2.625 - 2.5θ - 2θ^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048615} {:db/id 17592186193196 :question/id #uuid "20764fa3-2ba8-5be8-9509-089bf2a43562" :question/math-academy-id "q-159785"} {:db/id 17592186193197 :question/id #uuid "8bc6c054-1c5a-5b5e-aead-e667f2d931c5" :question/math-academy-id "q-159786"} {:db/id 17592186192797 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192521 :question/id #uuid "2ff20920-30c5-5027-b461-31b13d2031e5" :question/math-academy-id "e-11121"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6068f85b-0ea6-5161-a8d1-d4eb2504852b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050018}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186192985 :question/id #uuid "0df3572a-0fd0-5a5c-b2e0-870107821e66" :question/math-academy-id "q-143475"} {:db/id 17592186193195 :question/id #uuid "cee2f557-b129-5694-8dac-fc10e355c8aa" :question/math-academy-id "q-159781"}] :knowledge-point/title "Likelihood Functions for Exponential Random Variables"} {:db/id 17592186192521 :question/id #uuid "2ff20920-30c5-5027-b461-31b13d2031e5" :question/math-academy-id "e-11121" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186192797 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6068f85b-0ea6-5161-a8d1-d4eb2504852b" :knowledge-point/title "Likelihood Functions for Exponential Random Variables"}] :question/problem "Suppose $X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_6$ is an I.I.D random sample with $X_i \sim \text{Exp}(\theta)$ and unknown rate parameter $\theta$. Find the likelihood function of the sample $1.5, \, 2.0, \, 1.1, \, 0.4, \, 3.3, \, 2.7$." :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x; \theta)$, where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is

$$
L(\theta) = P(X_1=x_1, X_2=x_2, \ldots, X_n = x_n) = \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta)
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=6$ independent exponential random variables with unknown parameter $\theta$, for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x; \,\theta) = \theta e^{-\theta x}, \qquad x\geq 0
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
L(θ) &= ∏_(i = 1)^(n)θe^{- θx_{i}} \\
&= (θe^{- θx_{1}}) \cdot (θe^{- θx_{2}})⋯(θe^{- θx_{n}}) \\
&= θ^{n}e^{- θ(x_{1} + x_{2} + ⋯ + x_{n})} \\
&= θ^{n}e^{- θ∑x_{i}} \\
&= θ^{n}e^{-Sθ}
\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
\displaystyle S = \sum\limits_ {i=1}^n x_i
$$

For our sample, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}
S &= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} \\
&= 1.5 + 2.0 + 1.1 + 0.4 + 3.3 + 2.7 \\
&= 11
\end{aligned}
$$

and $n=6$. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
L(θ) &= θ^{6}e^{-11θ}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050018} {:db/id 17592186192985 :question/id #uuid "0df3572a-0fd0-5a5c-b2e0-870107821e66" :question/math-academy-id "q-143475"} {:db/id 17592186193195 :question/id #uuid "cee2f557-b129-5694-8dac-fc10e355c8aa" :question/math-academy-id "q-159781"} {:db/id 17592186192799 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192523 :question/id #uuid "bd63ff93-762d-5d7d-be8d-9701130b9fe5" :question/math-academy-id "e-11123"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cbba4fae-4e47-5a69-a6c1-d8754c18767a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048485} {:db/id 17592186049638}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186192986 :question/id #uuid "40dfb737-da3f-54c6-bef8-a8e5f7251e22" :question/math-academy-id "q-143497"} {:db/id 17592186193201 :question/id #uuid "3058acb9-d471-587a-a178-41dd1d63905c" :question/math-academy-id "q-159849"}] :knowledge-point/title "Likelihood Functions for Continuous Random Variables"} {:db/id 17592186192523 :question/id #uuid "bd63ff93-762d-5d7d-be8d-9701130b9fe5" :question/math-academy-id "e-11123" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186192799 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cbba4fae-4e47-5a69-a6c1-d8754c18767a" :knowledge-point/title "Likelihood Functions for Continuous Random Variables"}] :question/problem "Let $X_1, X_2, X_3$ be I.I.D. random variables with probability density function

Find the likelihood function of the sample $2.0, \, 4.5, \,5.1$." :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x; \theta)$, where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is

$$
L(\theta) = P(X_1=x_1, X_2=x_2, \ldots, X_n = x_n) = \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta)
$$

$$
f(x; \theta) = (\theta+1) x^{-\theta-2}, \qquad x \geq 1
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
L(θ) &= ∏_(i = 1)^(n)((θ + 1)x_{i}^{- θ - 2}) \\
&= (θ + 1)^{n} \cdot ∏_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}^{- θ - 2} \\
&= (θ + 1)^{n}(∏_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i})^{- θ - 2}
\end{aligned}
$$

For our sample, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}
∏_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} &= 2.0 \cdot 4.5 \cdot 5.1 = 45.9
\end{aligned}
$$

and $n=3$. Therefore,

$$
L(\theta) = (\theta+1)^{3} (45.9)^{-\theta-2}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048485} {:db/id 17592186049638} {:db/id 17592186192986 :question/id #uuid "40dfb737-da3f-54c6-bef8-a8e5f7251e22" :question/math-academy-id "q-143497"} {:db/id 17592186193201 :question/id #uuid "3058acb9-d471-587a-a178-41dd1d63905c" :question/math-academy-id "q-159849" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186192799 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cbba4fae-4e47-5a69-a6c1-d8754c18767a" :knowledge-point/title "Likelihood Functions for Continuous Random Variables"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a58a0ec5-d370-5b08-8b35-9d6e58770be7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "θ^{4}(33.6)^{- θ}" :db/id 17592186191093} {:answer/id #uuid "ed701c40-3275-56a0-9d82-0895adf0c693" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "θ^{3}(33.6)^{- θ - 1}" :db/id 17592186191094} {:answer/id #uuid "f1808a54-54a8-5581-8838-f23c49a9305a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "θ^{33.6}(4)^{- θ}" :db/id 17592186191095} {:answer/id #uuid "00c515da-8777-525e-bf01-7a36de740485" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "θ^{33.6}(4)^{- θ - 1}" :db/id 17592186191096} {:answer/id #uuid "6d5694b0-2319-5762-8044-e523c01a6149" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "θ^{33.6}(3)^{- θ - 1}" :db/id 17592186191097}] :answer-field/id #uuid "16f75826-a1b7-51cc-b472-78495d53facc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186191092}] :question/problem "Let $X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3}$ be I.I.D. random variables with probability density function

The only difference is that we use probability density functions instead of probability mass functions.

If $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed *continuous* random variables with probability density function $f(x; \theta)$, then the likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is given by

$$
L(\theta) = P(X_1=x_1, X_2=x_2, \ldots, X_n = x_n) = \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta)
$$

For example, let $X_1, X_2, X_3$ be continuous, I.I.D. random variables with the following probability density function:

$$
f(x; \theta) = \theta x^{-\theta-1}, \qquad x \geq 1
$$

Here, $\theta$ is an unknown parameter. Suppose we conduct our random sample and get the following results:

$$
x_1 = 2.5, \qquad x_2 = 3.2, \qquad x_3 = 1.2
$$

In this case, we compute the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
L(θ) &= ∏_(i = 1)^(n)(θx_{i}^{- θ - 1}) \\
&= (θx_{1}^{- θ - 1}) \cdot (θx_{2}^{- θ - 1})⋯(θx_{n}^{- θ - 1}) \\
&= θ^{n}(x_{1}^{- θ - 1}) \cdot (x_{2}^{- θ - 1})⋯(x_{n}^{- θ - 1}) \\
&= θ^{n}(x_{1} \cdot x_{2}⋯x_{n})^{- θ - 1} \\
&= θ^{n}(∏_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i})^{- θ - 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

For our sample, we have $n=3$, and

$$
\begin{aligned}
∏_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} &= 2.5 \cdot 3.2 \cdot 1.2 = 9.6
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
L(\theta) = \theta^{3} (9.6)^{-\theta-1}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5e339526-e303-5047-8def-188a04dca982" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7001 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7a3131cc-aeb5-5d42-af4a-921157386704" :step/math-academy-id 42268 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193687}} {:db/id 17592186193685 :step/content {:db/id 17592186192797 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192521 :question/id #uuid "2ff20920-30c5-5027-b461-31b13d2031e5" :question/math-academy-id "e-11121"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6068f85b-0ea6-5161-a8d1-d4eb2504852b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050018}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186192985} {:db/id 17592186193195}] :knowledge-point/title "Likelihood Functions for Exponential Random Variables"} :step/id #uuid "9623ba3e-7523-5921-af5c-689ea499d4b4" :step/math-academy-id 42283 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193692}} {:db/id 17592186193687 :step/content {:db/id 17592186192799 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192523 :question/id #uuid "bd63ff93-762d-5d7d-be8d-9701130b9fe5" :question/math-academy-id "e-11123"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cbba4fae-4e47-5a69-a6c1-d8754c18767a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048485} {:db/id 17592186049638}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186192986} {:db/id 17592186193201}] :knowledge-point/title "Likelihood Functions for Continuous Random Variables"} :step/id #uuid "bc09f530-58a5-566a-a408-bd7b51bd761e" :step/math-academy-id 42301 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193685}} {:db/id 17592186193692 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193902 :tutorial/content "The probability density function of a normally distributed random variable $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ is given by

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac12\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2}
$$

Some example normal distribution curves are shown below.

![](images/c9/c9359fc84401aabb19e526755b70647cb0496fa8ddba65974466e0ffc3dbbbdc.png)

If we set $\sigma=1$, then $f(x)$ simplifies as follows:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2}
$$

This is a standard normal random variable whose mean is shifted right by $\mu$ units.

Finally, setting the unknown parameter as $\theta$ when discussing likelihood functions is common. Following this convention, we set $\mu=\theta$, and we get

$$
f(x;\theta) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-\theta)^2/2}
$$

Let's use this to compute some likelihood functions of some normally distributed sample data." :tutorial/id #uuid "8e08170d-c55e-531f-a8b9-99dfa8ecbac7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7019 :tutorial/title "The Normal Distribution"} :step/id #uuid "5912947a-0cd6-5e5a-958c-a4fff1dab140" :step/math-academy-id 42321 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193505}}] :activity/title "Likelihood Functions for Continuous Probability Distributions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186192932} {:db/id 17592186193681 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193897 :tutorial/content "Likelihood functions of samples drawn from populations modeled using continuous random variables are defined similarly to discrete variables. &= (θx_{1}^{- θ - 1}) \cdot (θx_{2}^{- θ - 1})⋯(θx_{n}^{- θ - 1}) \\
&= θ^{n}(x_{1}^{- θ - 1}) \cdot (x_{2}^{- θ - 1})⋯(x_{n}^{- θ - 1}) \\
&= θ^{n}(x_{1} \cdot x_{2}⋯x_{n})^{- θ - 1} \\
&= θ^{n}(∏_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i})^{- θ - 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

For our sample, we have $n=3$, and

$$
\begin{aligned}
∏_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} &= 2.5 \cdot 3.2 \cdot 1.2 = 9.6
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
L(\theta) = \theta^{3} (9.6)^{-\theta-1}

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac12\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2}
$$

Some example normal distribution curves are shown below.

![](images/c9/c9359fc84401aabb19e526755b70647cb0496fa8ddba65974466e0ffc3dbbbdc.png)

If we set $\sigma=1$, then $f(x)$ simplifies as follows:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2}
$$

This is a standard normal random variable whose mean is shifted right by $\mu$ units.

Finally, setting the unknown parameter as $\theta$ when discussing likelihood functions is common. Following this convention, we set $\mu=\theta$, and we get

$$
f(x;\theta) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-\theta)^2/2}
$$

17592186045417] [17592186046658 1008 "Our Mathematics for Machine Learning course provides a comprehensive foundation of the essential mathematical tools required to study modern machine learning.
This course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.
On completing this course, students will be well-prepared for a university-level machine learning course that tackles concepts such as gradient descent, neural networks, backpropagation, support vector machines, naive Bayes classifiers, and Gaussian mixture models." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics in set theory and logic. Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network.
Students then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.
As part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.
Students will learn how to find eigenvectors of a matrix, compute matrix diagonalizations, and extend these ideas to orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices. These techniques underpin dimensionality reduction methods and are central to understanding the structure of data.
The course then develops key applications of linear algebra in machine learning. Students study singular value decomposition and its relationship to principal component analysis, and learn how these tools are used for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and identifying structure in high-dimensional datasets. Linear least-squares problems and regression techniques are also studied as foundational methods for fitting models to data.
A solid grasp of multivariable calculus is essential for understanding modern machine learning algorithms. In this course, students become well-versed in partial derivatives and gradient vectors (used in gradient-based optimization), the multivariable chain rule (essential for backpropagation), and vector-valued functions. Students extend differentiation to maps between multi-dimensional vector spaces and develop the tools of vector and matrix calculus used to compute gradients of loss functions in neural networks.
Students also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning.
Students work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions.
On the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail.
Students extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling.
The course concludes with parametric inference, focusing on point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals, which form the statistical foundation for many machine learning In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta$ and variance

$$

$$

for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x; \theta) = \dfrac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{x-\theta}{\sigma} \right)^2} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(x-\theta)^2/2}, \qquad x \in (-\infty,\infty)

$$

&= (2π)^{-n/2}e^{- (C - 2Sθ + nθ^{2})/2}
\end{aligned}

$$
\displaystyle S = \sum\limits_ {i=1}^n x_i

$$

&= 5.25
\end{aligned}
$$

&= θ^{n}(x_{1} \cdot x_{2}⋯x_{n})^{- θ - 1} \\

\end{aligned}
